sweep_summary: Both title-hits are on target and were read in full. Bennett 2013 (Phonology 30: 355-398; CUP copy closed, author-hosted PDF open, saved) states the rule categorically ('Stress the ultima if heavy, otherwise the penult', p. 357) with lexical exceptions (25% of bisyllabic light-final nouns/adjectives oxytone, twelve antepenult nouns, no verbs; p. 358) but explicitly adopts Parker's description without critique. Parker 1998 (Glottolog 116705) is the UMass generals paper printed unrevised in GIALens 7(1) 2013; it was on file with a garbled text layer, which I decoded this sweep (font shift +1, U+F020 = space) so the passages are quotable: sec. 3.1 pp. 5-6 gives the same first-hand rule, quantifies the exceptions (56/225 = 24.9% of bisyllabic light-final nouns/adjectives), and pp. 22-23 add the twelve antepenult nouns and the three-syllable window. Also fetched sources Bennett's 2013 handout (same facts) and re-read the catalog's Parker 1992 pp. 5-6 from the page images, which confirm the catalog quote and correct three scanned misreads (tajpin, paloma, majshó; ríshquiti stressed on the antepenult). Not obtainable: Parker 1998b SIL WP 42 (Cloudflare 403; abstract says it is a duration study of coda [h], not stress placement; low priority) and Parker 1994 IJAL (paywalled DOI 10.1086/466224; medium priority, first-hand but redundant with 1998a for placement). Bearing on the catalog: the weight-sensitive coding is confirmed; the hedge is better expressed as lexical exceptions than as an uncertain weight rule, and Parker 1998a p. 6 is recommended as the deciding first-hand quotation with Parker 1992 as the corroborating primary document.

new_statements.quote: To summarize our findings thus far, the basic pattern is that primary stress in Huariapano falls on the final syllable of the word if it is heavy (closed by a coda consonant), and otherwise on the penultimate. [...] Nevertheless, in spite of this basic, default pattern of penultimate stress in words whose final syllable is underlyingly open, there exist a number of exceptional forms which surface with primary stress on the final syllable, even though it is light. [...] within a list of 225 bisyllabic nouns and adjectives, 169 of them (75.1 percent) exhibit regular penultimate stress, whereas the remaining 56 words (24.9 percent) surface phonetically with stress on a light ultima [...] none of them are verbs.

new_statements.reading: First-hand statement by the fieldworker whose 1992 orthography note is the catalog's deciding source. Weight-sensitive right-edge stress: closed final syllable takes stress ('always attracts the stress', p. 5); otherwise penult; word-final transitional [h]-type segments do not count as codas (fn. 5). Exceptions are lexical, not weight-driven: 24.9% of bisyllabic light-final nouns/adjectives are oxytone, twelve nouns are proparoxytone (pp. 22-23), no verb is exceptional, and primary stress always falls within the last three syllables. This turns the 1992 'normalmente... normalmente' hedges into a categorical heavy-ultima rule plus a bounded, noun-only set of lexical exceptions; Bennett 2013 (pp. 357-358) restates the same facts as rule (5) 'Stress the ultima if heavy, otherwise the penult'. Consistent with the catalog's weight-sensitive coding; the 'hedged' element is best recoded as lexical exceptions (roughly a quarter of light-final disyllabic nouns) rather than as uncertainty about the weight rule.

audit.reasoning: Both halves of the deciding quotation are verbatim in held files (Parker 1992 orthography note, Rosetta scanned and full SIL 2008 re-edition pp. 5-6; Bennett 2013 Phonology 30 p. 357). The language is extinct and Parker is its sole modern describer; no reference grammar exists (Glottolog: 5 descriptive refs, none a grammar; Navarro 1903 held, no stress rule). sources.note: Translation: 'In Huariapano the prosodic accent normally falls on the penultimate syllable of the word... However, when a word ends in a consonant, the accent normally moves to the last syllable... Words whose accentuation does not conform to these two rules are marked with an acute accent on the stressed syllable to help the non-native reader. Examples: majshó "fox", ríshquiti "whip".' sources.quote: Huariapano, an extinct language of Peru, exhibits an unusual process of coda epenthesis by which the segment [h] is inserted in odd-numbered syllables of the prosodic word. [...] This article presents the results of an instrumental study which indicates that insofar as their relative duration is concerned, syllable-final [h]'s in Huariapano pattern as fully moraic coda consonants in keeping with the trochaic constraint HeavyFootHead.
sources.note: The only acoustic study of the language (rhyme/coda-[h] duration); bears on the moraic status of codas, i.e. the weight criterion behind the CVC-heavy coding; open on UND Scholarly Commons but Cloudflare blocks scripted download.
